prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms made timekeeping at the 10^-18 level possible

statement.case_for: I have moved from B007 to B056 as my sole preferred part. The reason is not the support count, which I do not treat as evidence, but that the round-1 exchange exposed a structural problem in my own first choice that the clock does not share. The clock also meets the test I applied to topological insulators: it rests on one simple, general mechanism. If the light that holds the atoms shifts both clock levels equally (the magic wavelength), the trap drops out of the measurement and thousands of atoms can be interrogated with Doppler and recoil effects suppressed. That idea is Katori's. Ye's group took it to the 1e-18 frontier and tied it to the comb. The result has been reproduced and surpassed independently at several laboratories, and it is understood quantitatively, since the light-shift theory predicts what the experiments find. It also now gives physics beyond accuracy: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, tighter limits on drifting constants, and sensitivity to ultralight dark matter. Credit is carried by two names that every member proposed, which is a cleaner defence than any three-name version of B007 I can write.
statement.case_against: The reservations I raised in round 1 about the clock have been answered only in part. It is still an invention and a measurement capability, and the physics it enables (redshift, constants, dark matter) is promising but has so far produced limits and demonstrations rather than a surprise. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize are real overlaps, and a critic can call this a refinement of recognised precision spectroscopy. Two names cannot cover Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom or the PTB, NIST and SYRTE teams, and a citation must be worded to honour the lattice-clock concept without implying that they did not contribute. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so waiting would cost little. For B007, my abandoned first choice, I still think the science is stronger as a discovery of a new class of matter; I leave it only because the credit cannot be resolved within three names.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock does more than improve accuracy: it opens new measurements of gravity and constants, and he objects to weighting understanding over observation. He also notes that a two-part prize including B007 would need more than three names.
responses.response: That is a fair rebuke and I accept it. My question in round 1, whether the clock is a new principle or a superb realisation of a known one, was too narrow. Magic-wavelength trapping is a new principle in my sense: a general condition under which an apparently uncontrollable perturbation cancels exactly, and then the whole architecture follows from it. I also accept his count: B056 plus B007 would need five names, so I no longer propose a two-part prize. Where I still ask for care is the citation. It should name the lattice clock concept and its development, not time-keeping in general, so that the ion-clock and comb work already honoured is not claimed again.

responses.point: Lindroth asks whether the quantum spin Hall effect can be separated cleanly from the three-dimensional topological insulator story, and says she would find the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio more convincing if it can. She treats B007 as a serious competitor to the clock.
responses.response: I thought hard about her question and my answer is that it can be separated in the physics but not in the credit. The Z2 classification and the helical edge state are a self-contained 2D story. The 3D materials, with Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and the ARPES groups, are a second story, and a citation limited to the quantum spin Hall effect would be honest. The difficulty is what it implies for the prediction: the HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is what made Molenkamp's experiment possible, and Zhang cannot be honoured because he has died. That makes a three-person B007 defensible only if we are willing to say publicly why two of the key theorists are absent. I am not sure we should accept that when a two-name alternative of comparable standing exists, and this tipped my vote.

responses.point: Eriksson, who also prefers B007, asks the committee to settle whether the prize centres on the quantum spin Hall effect, where Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are natural names, or on topological insulators in general, where the 3D work would have to be included. He calls the trio a deliberate cut through a larger field.
responses.response: I agree with the framing, and it is the reason I now think B007 is not ready for a three-name credit. If the prize centres on the quantum spin Hall effect, the natural prediction credit becomes Kane and Mele plus Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the experimental credit Molenkamp, which exceeds three even before the 3D work. If it centres on topological insulators in general, the Fu-Kane-Mele and Moore-Balents work and the ARPES groups enter. A deliberate cut is acceptable, but I do not see a cut that I could explain without a footnote that undermines it. I would still want us to return to B007 once there is a configuration that fits the three-name limit, and I share his view that the discovery itself is mature.

responses.point: Danielsson says he would not oppose a later year for topological insulators, but sees the clock as having cleaner attribution and broader support, with no need to wait for the redefinition of the second. He also says the clock is not just a better clock but a probe of redshift, constants and dark matter.
responses.response: I now agree with him on both timing and framing. On timing, the performance is confirmed across laboratories, so waiting for the formal redefinition of the second would add a ceremony and nothing to the evidence. On framing, I want the argument for the clock to rest on the physics it opens and not on the engineering, because the committee's emphasis is on discovery. I would add one condition: the case should be made on what has already been measured (millimetre-scale redshift, comparisons across fibre links, constraints on constants), not on what the clocks might find after the redefinition.

responses.point: Olsson, who prefers B032, challenges the B007 trio because the HgTe observation verified someone else's proposal, and she notes the overlap with the 2016 prize. She asks whether three names can do justice to both prediction and observation.
responses.response: Her sequence-of-credit point is correct and I have taken it on board: the experiment followed the BHZ prediction. On the 2016 overlap I still disagree, because time-reversal-invariant Z2 topology is not the same thing as the integer quantum Hall-type topology honoured then, but the overlap is arguable. On B032, I accept the strength of the documented chain from Rose's design to Haider's corrector to Urban's gains, and I keep it as an alternative. I would still ask her to address the Nion line of Batson, Dellby and Krivanek, because the clock's two-name credit is cleaner than a B032 trio that leaves out an independent success.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the lattice clock as a discovery-level achievement in the Nobel sense, given that all five supporters accept it is an invention and measurement capability.
Whether the citation can honour Katori's lattice concept and Ye's development without implying that Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups did not contribute.

Whether a future B007 configuration can handle the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang prediction, given that Zhang cannot receive the prize, and whether the 2016 prize and the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize change its timing.
Whether my change from B007 to B056 reflects a better judgement of credit or my own bias toward whichever theory-led mechanism I find simplest.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any candidate. I share a Gothenburg physics environment with Johansson and Olsson (Chalmers) but have no collaboration with Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or the B032 names. My earlier note about a possible bias toward theory-led work still applies: it favoured B007 and I have discounted it. My research field is statistical physics of complex systems and not atomic physics, so I rely on Lindroth and Kroll for the details of the clock.
